validator: draft 1 passes with no problems, soft points or warnings
keep: The idea is named up front: a magnet turning inside fixed coils, one cycle per north-and-south passing, three coils giving three waves 120° apart.

The causal step is there: the flux through a coil rises, falls and reverses as a north then a south pole passes, and a coil makes voltage only while that flux changes, so a parked pole makes nothing (screen 2 shows that side of the rule).

The picture is the brief's turning field: a rotor with 2, 4 or 6 poles inside a stator with a set of three coils per pole pair, drag or Play, three traces building, a speed slider moving frequency and voltage together and a field-current slider moving the voltage alone.

One rule computes every readout: f = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60 and voltage = 440 × (f ÷ 60) × (field ÷ 100%), from E = 4.44 f N Φ taught in Transformers. 57 Hz and 418 V at 1710 rev/min are worked from it.

Both misconceptions in the brief have a DO screen with its own hint: poles for pole pairs (screen 8 with 120 Hz and 30 Hz as slips, screen 12 with 500 and 2000 rev/min) and the field current changing the frequency (screen 10). Screen 2 adds a DC field expected to give a DC output.

Twelve screens: SHOW 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 alternate with DO 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ending on two mixed typed puzzles (11, 12). Every figure answer is typed (6.67 ms, 3 cycles, 60 Hz, 396 V, 1000 rev/min) with its wrong options as slips. Every SHOW screen is under 90 words.
Every SHOW screen that asks for a drag or a tap has a Read and a Still; every DO Read only restates its question.
The analogy, a toothed wheel past a sensor, reproduces the rule (clicks a second = teeth × rev/min ÷ 60) and says where it breaks, which is exactly the poles-or-pole-pairs trap.
fix: False absolute: 'An alternator is a magnet turning inside fixed coils' and 'The coils stay still' are not true of every alternator. The brushless exciter in the next lesson turns its coils, and a PMG's rotor is a permanent magnet. Say a generator set's main alternator, and add to the ignores that some small machines turn their coils instead.

Claim that fails after a later idea: the takeaway's 'the speed sets the frequency and the field current moves the voltage alone' is false in parallel (lesson 6: more fuel barely moves the frequency, more field moves kVAr). Say the frequency is locked to the speed, and the field current changes only the voltage the coils make. The explanation's speed and field sentences and the practice's proportion rule get 'on a set running alone with nothing connected'.
The takeaway's 'three fixed coils 120° apart' is true only of a 2-pole machine; a 4-pole stator's coils are 60° apart. Say the coils make three phases 120° apart, and cite the 120° quote there.
